title: The biggest class: nouns with no plural and adjectives that hum
goal: Buy clothes, name colors, bargain over prices — and master the noun class with the most members, whose singular and plural forms are identical.
bekal: the N class: *nyumba*, *nguo*, *safari* — singular and plural look the same
the subject prefix of this class: *i-* for one, *zi-* for many

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kununua nguo sokoni
dialogs.intro: There's a party invitation for the weekend. Amina takes Budi to the cloth market to find something to wear.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Unahitaji nguo mpya kwa sherehe ya Jumamosi.
lines.id: You need new clothes for Saturday's party.
lines.literal: you-are-needing clothes new for party of Saturday.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kweli. Nguo zangu zote ni chafu kidogo.
lines.id: True. My clothes are all a bit dirty.
lines.literal: true. clothes of-me all are dirty a-little.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Angalia nguo hizi. Rangi gani unapenda?
lines.id: Look at these clothes. What color do you like?
lines.literal: look clothes these. color which you-are-liking?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ninapenda rangi ya bluu. Nguo hii ni bei gani?
lines.id: I like blue. How much is this outfit?
lines.literal: I-am-liking color of blue. clothes this is price which?

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.text: Elfu ishirini. Ni nguo nzuri sana, safi kabisa.
lines.id: Twenty thousand. It's very nice clothing, perfectly neat.
lines.literal: thousand twenty. is clothes good very, clean completely.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ghali sana! Punguza bei kidogo, tafadhali.
lines.id: Very expensive! Please lower the price a little.
lines.literal: expensive very! reduce price a-little, please.

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.text: Kwa sababu wewe ni rafiki: elfu kumi na tano.
lines.id: Because you're a friend: fifteen thousand.
lines.literal: for reason you are friend: thousand ten and five.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sawa. Na kanga hizi ni ngapi?
lines.id: Okay. And how much are these kangas?
lines.literal: okay. and kangas these are how-many?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Kanga ni nzuri kwa mama yako! Zina maneno mazuri.
lines.id: A kanga would be perfect for your mother! They have lovely sayings on them.
lines.literal: kanga is good for mother of-you! they-have words good.

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.text: Kanga mbili ni elfu kumi tu. Rangi zote ziko hapa.
lines.id: Two kangas are only ten thousand. All colors are here.
lines.literal: kanga two is thousand ten only. colors all they-are-located here.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ninachukua kanga mbili nyekundu na nguo moja ya bluu.
lines.id: I'll take two red kangas and one blue outfit.
lines.literal: I-am-taking kanga two red and clothes one of blue.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Bei nzuri sana! Sasa una nguo za sherehe.
lines.id: A very good price! Now you have party clothes.
lines.literal: price good very! now you-have clothes of party.

notes: **Bei gani? is how you ask a price.** Literally "price which?". Synonyms: *Ni pesa ngapi?* (how much money?) and the shortest: *Ngapi?*. Bargaining at the market is not rude in East Africa — it is part of the conversation, and sellers actually wait for you to haggle.

**Punguza bei means "lower the price".** Natural bargaining lines: *Punguza kidogo* (lower it a bit), *Bei ya mwisho ni ngapi?* (what's the final price?), *Nitalipa elfu kumi* (I'll pay ten thousand). The command form is set up in unit 14.

**Kwa sababu means "because", and you already know half of it.** *Sababu* is Arabic *sabab*, "reason". *Kwa* means "with; for; by" and will turn up everywhere: *kwa nini?* (why?), *kwa sababu* (because), *kwa ajili ya* (for the sake of).

**Zote means "all" for this class.** The word *-ote* follows the noun class: *wote* (all people), *vyote* (all ki- things), *zote* (all N-class things), *yote* (all gari-class things). You've been using *wote* since unit 1.

**A kanga is a rectangular printed cloth that always carries a saying.** A kanga is always sold as a pair — one for the waist, one for the shoulders or head. The saying along the edge (*jina la kanga*) can be a proverb, a prayer, or a gentle dig at a neighbor. Buying a kanga without reading its saying is a tourist mistake that locals love to laugh about.

grammars.title: The N class: singular and plural alike
body: This class has the most members, and it is both the easiest and the most deceptive. Easy, because **the singular and plural forms are identical**: *nyumba* means "house" and "houses". Deceptive, because its adjectives change shape in a way you have to hear, not memorize.

head: Adjective
N-class form
Sound rule
Example
rows: n- before z, d, g, j
no prefix before k, t, f, s, ch

after: The rule really fits in one sentence: **the n sound adapts itself to the next letter, and disappears if it can't blend in**. Before *b*, *p*, *v* it becomes *m*; before a vowel it becomes *ny*; before a hard letter like *k*, *t*, *f*, *s*, *ch* it vanishes altogether. Your tongue already knows this rule from English: *in-* becomes *im-* before *p* and *b* (*impossible*, *imbalance*), and *in-* + *r* becomes *ir-* (*irregular*).
Arabic-loan adjectives don't take part at all: *nguo safi*, *habari muhimu*, *safari tayari*, *kazi ngumu*. Nothing to add in front.

⚠️ Don't be thrown by *nyumba nzuri mbili* — three words, three different rules, all correct: *nzuri* gets *n-*, *mbili* uses its bare form because that is how this class works, and *nyumba* doesn't change because singular and plural are the same.

grammars.title: The subject prefixes i- and zi-
body: Things in this class have their own subject prefix when they are the subject of a sentence: **i-** for one, **zi-** for many. This is the part that surprises new learners most — the verb changes to match the noun class, not just the adjective.
after: Possessives and the connector follow the same pattern: **yangu / zangu** and **ya / za**. *Nguo yangu* (my clothes, one item) → *nguo zangu* (my clothes, many). *Nguo ya sherehe* (a party outfit) → *nguo za sherehe* (party clothes).
You saw the demonstratives in unit 6: *hii* / *hizi* (this), *hiyo* / *hizo* (that, just mentioned), *ile* / *zile* (that over there).

Because this class takes in nearly all loanwords — *meza*, *chai*, *hoteli*, *simu*, *picha*, *saa*, *kazi*, *bei*, *pesa*, *safari*, *habari*, *shilingi* — *i-*, *zi-*, *ya*, *za* and *nzuri* are the sounds you will hear most in everyday Swahili. If you had to pick one class to learn thoroughly, pick this one.

blocks.text: The verb is *kuvaa* (to wear): *Ninavaa kanzu* (I'm wearing a kanzu), *Anavaa kofia* (he/she is wearing a cap). To take off: *kuvua* — notice only one letter differs, and the same word also means "to fish".

In Zanzibar and along the Tanzanian coast, modest dress is more than a suggestion. Women cover their shoulders and knees, and men don't go shirtless away from the beach. A *kanga* or *kitenge* wrapped around the waist is the most practical solution — and doubles as a souvenir.

Every kanga carries a sentence printed along its edge. The sentence has a name of its own, *jina la kanga*, and is often used to say something that is awkward to say out loud. A few of the best known — and you can read all of them now:

head: Saying on the kanga
English
rows: Love is a matter of the heart
Thank you, Mother, for raising me
Come, guest, so that the host may prosper

blocks.text: *Baraka* (blessing, from Arabic *baraka*), *fitina* (Arabic *fitna*; gossip, discord), *penzi* from *kupenda* — once again, some of the words are already familiar before you opened this course.

The last proverb explains something about East Africa that you will feel for yourself: a guest is considered to bring a blessing, not a burden. That is why the word *karibu* is said so often, and said so sincerely.
